Problem[edit]

A stack of cards is labelled with the integers from to with different integers on different cards. The cards in the stack are not in numerical order. The top card is removed from the stack and placed on the table, and the next card is moved to the bottom of the stack. The new top card is removed from the stack and placed on the table, to the right of the card already there, and the next card in the stack is moved to the bottom of the stack. The process - placing the top card to the right of the cards already on the table and moving the next card in the stack to the bottom of the stack - is repeated until all cards are on the table. It is found that, reading from left to right, the labels on the cards are now in ascending order: In the original stack of cards, how many cards were above the card labeled ?

Solution 1[edit]

We try to work backwards from when there are 2 cards left, since this is when the 1999 card is laid onto the table. When there are 2 cards left, the 1999 card is on the top of the deck. In order for this to occur, it must be 2nd on the deck when there are 4 cards remaining, and this means it must be the 4th card when there are 8 cards remaining. This pattern continues until it is the 512th card on the deck when there are 1024 cards remaining. Since there are over 1000 cards remaining, some cards have not even made one trip through yet, , to be exact. Once these cards go through, 1999 will be the card on the deck. Since every other card was removed during the first round, it goes to show that 1999 was in position , meaning that there were cards are above the one labeled .

To simplify matters, we want a power of . Hence, we will add 'fake' cards which we must discard in our actual count. Using similar logic as Solution 1, we find that 1999 has position in a card stack, where the fake cards towards the front.

Let the fake cards have positions . Then, we know that the real cards filling the gaps between the fake cards must be the cards such that they go to their correct starting positions in the card case, where all of them are below . From this, we know that the cards from positions to alternate in fake-real-fake-real, where we have the correct order of cards once the first have moved and we can start putting real cards on the table. Hence, is in position , so cards are above it. - Spacesam

Next, let's think about how we can construct a stack of cards from a stack of cards. First, let us renumber the current stack of by adding to the label of each of the cards. Then we must add a card labeled "" somewhere in the new deck.

Working backwards, we find that we must move the bottom card to the top, then add "" to the top of the deck. This is because after one move, the number "" will be laid out and the top card will be moved to the bottom, so the deck becomes the same as what we had before, but with everything renumbered correctly such that will then be laid out in order.

Therefore, if (meaning the card is not at the bottom of the deck and so it won't be moved to the top), then , since a card from the bottom is moved to be above the card, and the new card "" is added to the top. If (meaning the card is the bottom card), then because the card will move to the top and the card "" will be added on top of it.

Solution 6 (Bashing with Modular Arithmetic)[edit]

Similar to Solution 5, we treat each run-through of the deck from the lowest-indexed card to the highest-indexed card as a separate round. Notice that after each round, approximately half the deck will remain, with the other half having been cast aside to the right in sorted order. Then, we can model each round as if we are running a "Sieve" through the deck with powers of 2s, filtering out the cards to put to the right and the cards to be pushed to the bottom.

At the beginning, when all cards are still in the deck, notice that the first run-through of the deck consists of removing all the cards such that their index , while we leave behind all the cards such that their index . (Since the cards are not -indexed, using instead of is simpler to keep track of the cards. This will appear again later.) The remaining cards, then, will all share the attribute that their index numbers are even. To split this further for round 2, we look more specifically at each index, categorizing them further as or in that order (The card with the smaller remainder will always be the card on the top of the new deck). Then, in Round 2, we will remove all the cards with index values that leave a remainder of when divided by , while leaving the multiples of behind. Notice that each time, in each new deck, we are removing all the cards with an odd position in that specific deck, and leaving behind all the cards with an even position in that specific deck.

This process will continue until we reach Round 5, where the number of cards that remain () is no longer a multiple of 2. Therefore, when we remove all the cards with indices and leave behind all the cards with indices , the last card in the deck will be removed instead of being placed to the bottom, with cards remaining. Because of this, when Round 6 begins, we cannot follow our normal procedure, since the top card of the Round 6 deck would have been moved to the bottom! Therefore, when we are using our sieve with and , the order at which the remainders are presented have flipped, so all the cards with indices that are multiples of 64 will be removed, while all the cards with indices that are 32 more than a multiple of 64 will remain. The cards from Round 6 will be reduced to , and the last card in the deck will be removed just like in Round 5, which means Round 7 will be affected the same way. Of the choices of and , we will remove the latter, leaving behind the cards with indices that are 32 more than a multiple of 128. However, since 31 is an odd number, the last card of the deck will NOT be removed, which means our sieving process will return to normal after Round 7, with cards remaining. Since is a perfect power of , we will not need to worry about this scenario again in the following rounds.

Round 8: removed; remains; cards left.

Round 9: removed; remains; cards left.

Round 10: removed; remains; cards left.

Round 11: removed; remains; card left.

Round 12: The last card in position is sorted into place (This is card #!).

It is obvious that the single card put into place in Round 11 is the second-to-last card in the deck, which is our target #. Then, its position in the original deck leaves a remainder of when divided by . It is easy to see that is the only index that satisfies this, so there will be cards above card #.
